questions.stem: What is a mixture?
options: A substance that cannot be separated
Two or more substances combined but not chemically joined
Two or more elements chemically bonded together
A substance made of only one type of atom
questions.explanation: In a mixture the substances keep their own properties and can be separated physically. Chemical bonding makes a compound instead.

questions.stem: What is a pure substance?
options: Any liquid with nothing floating in it
A substance made of only one type of particle throughout
A substance that is safe to drink
questions.explanation: In science 'pure' means one substance only, not 'clean' or 'healthy'. Pure water is one substance; clear tap water is a mixture.

questions.stem: What is a solution?
options: A mixture where particles settle at the bottom
A mixture where one substance is dissolved evenly in another
questions.explanation: A solution is uniform throughout, with the solute dissolved in the solvent.

questions.stem: In salty water, what is the solute?
questions.explanation: The solute dissolves; the solvent does the dissolving. Salt dissolves in water, so salt is the solute.
questions.teaching:
Every solution has a substance being dissolved and a substance doing the dissolving, and telling them apart is what most of these questions test.

The one that disappears into the other — the one you could recover by evaporating the mixture — is the solute. The one present in the larger amount, which stays in its own state, is the solvent. So for any solution, ask which component would be left behind as a residue if you boiled the mixture dry. That residue is the solute, and it is usually the substance named second in the mixture's everyday name.

questions.stem: What is a solvent?
options: The substance that does the dissolving
questions.explanation: Water is the most common solvent. The dissolved substance is the solute.

questions.stem: Which technique separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?
questions.explanation: Filtration traps particles too large to pass through the filter paper. It cannot separate a dissolved solid.
questions.teaching:
Choosing a separation technique means asking which physical property differs between the components.

If a solid will not dissolve in the liquid it is mixed with, the two remain physically distinct and the solid particles are simply larger than the gaps in a mesh or paper barrier. Pouring the mixture through leaves the solid behind and lets the liquid through. If the solid had dissolved, this would not work at all — you would need evaporation or distillation instead, since a dissolved solute passes straight through the barrier with the liquid.

questions.stem: Which technique would you use to get pure water from salty water?
questions.explanation: Distillation evaporates the water and condenses it again, leaving the salt behind. Filtration would not remove dissolved salt.

questions.stem: Which technique separates iron filings from sand?
questions.explanation: Iron is magnetic and sand is not, so a magnet exploits a difference in properties.
questions.teaching:
Separation techniques work by exploiting a physical difference between the components, so the method is chosen to match the difference available.

Filtration uses particle size, separating an insoluble solid from a liquid. Evaporation uses boiling point, recovering a dissolved solid. Distillation uses boiling point to recover the liquid instead. Chromatography uses how strongly substances stick to a surface. And where one component responds to a magnetic field and the other does not, that single property is enough on its own. Ask what physical property differs, and the technique follows.

questions.stem: What is chromatography used to separate?
options: Mixtures of coloured or dissolved substances, such as inks
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates dissolved substances by how far they travel through a medium.

questions.stem: What is a homogeneous mixture?
options: One with the same composition throughout
One made of a single element
questions.explanation: Homogeneous means uniform. A solution is the standard example.

questions.stem: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
questions.explanation: A salad has visibly different parts. The others are uniform throughout.
questions.teaching:
Mixtures are described by how evenly the components are distributed, and there are two categories.

In one, the components are so thoroughly and evenly mixed that any sample looks the same as any other, and you cannot pick out the separate parts — a solution of salt in water, or air. In the other, the components stay visibly distinct, so different samples can differ, and you can see or pick out the pieces. Sand and gravel, muesli, and a jar of oil and vinegar are all the second kind. The prefixes come from Greek: homo means same, hetero means different.

questions.stem: What happens to the salt when salty water is evaporated?
options: It is left behind as a solid
questions.explanation: Water has a much lower boiling point, so it leaves first and the salt stays.

questions.stem: What is the residue in filtration?
options: The solid trapped in the filter paper
questions.explanation: The residue stays behind; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.

questions.stem: What is the filtrate?
options: The liquid that passes through the filter
The solid left in the filter
questions.explanation: Filtrate is what comes through. Residue is what stays.

questions.stem: What does 'soluble' mean?
options: Able to dissolve in a given solvent
questions.explanation: Soluble substances dissolve. Insoluble ones do not, and can be filtered out.

questions.stem: Which of these is a pure substance?
questions.explanation: Distilled water is water only. Sea water, milk and air are all mixtures.
questions.teaching:
A pure substance contains only one kind of particle right through it — either a single element, or a single compound with a fixed composition.

Tap water fails this, because it contains dissolved minerals, chlorine and gases. Distillation removes those by boiling the water off and condensing the vapour, leaving impurities behind. So the useful question is not whether something looks clear or clean, but whether it has anything else mixed into it. Milk, seawater and air all look uniform to varying degrees and are all mixtures.

questions.stem: What is decantation?
options: Passing a mixture through filter paper
Using a magnet to remove metal
Pouring off a liquid and leaving settled solid behind
questions.explanation: Decanting relies on the solid settling first. It is quicker than filtering but less complete.

questions.stem: What is crystallisation used for?
options: Obtaining a dissolved solid as solid crystals
questions.explanation: Slowly evaporating the solvent lets the dissolved solid form crystals.

questions.stem: Which mixture would sieving separate best?
questions.explanation: Sieving separates solids by particle size. Dissolved or liquid mixtures need other methods.

questions.stem: What is an alloy?
options: A mixture of metals, or of a metal with another element
questions.explanation: Brass and steel are alloys — mixtures, not compounds, which is why their composition can be varied.

questions.stem: Why can distillation separate ethanol from water but filtration cannot?
options: Ethanol and water do not mix
They have different boiling points but both pass through filter paper
Ethanol is a solid at room temperature
questions.explanation: Filtration separates by particle size, and both liquids pass through. Distillation exploits the boiling point difference.

questions.stem: A student filters muddy water and the filtrate is still slightly brown. What does this show?
options: Some coloured substance is dissolved, so filtration cannot remove it
The filter paper was the wrong colour
questions.explanation: Dissolved substances pass through filter paper. Only suspended particles are trapped.

questions.stem: Which property does chromatography rely on?
options: Different substances are attracted to magnets
Different substances have different masses only
Different substances travel different distances through the medium
Different substances have different boiling points
questions.explanation: Separation depends on how strongly each substance is held by the paper versus carried by the solvent.

questions.stem: Why is air classified as a mixture rather than a compound?
options: Its gases are not chemically joined and its proportions can vary
questions.explanation: Air's composition varies from place to place, and its gases keep their own properties. A compound has a fixed ratio.

questions.stem: In distillation, what happens in the condenser?
options: Vapour is cooled back into a liquid
The liquid is heated to boiling
questions.explanation: The condenser cools the vapour so it returns to liquid and can be collected as the distillate.

questions.stem: Why does a solute dissolve faster in hot water?
options: Particles move faster, so they mix and break apart more quickly
Hot water is a stronger solvent chemically
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means faster particle motion and more frequent collisions. The solute is dissolving, not melting.

questions.stem: A mixture of sand, salt and water needs the sand and the salt recovered as solids. What is the correct order?
options: Filter to remove sand, then evaporate the filtrate to recover salt
questions.explanation: Sand is insoluble so it filters out first; the salt is dissolved in the filtrate and is recovered by evaporation.

questions.stem: Two ink spots travel different distances up chromatography paper. What can you conclude?
questions.explanation: Distance travelled is a property of the substance under those conditions, so different distances mean different substances.

questions.stem: Why must the ink spot sit above the solvent level in chromatography?
options: The spot would travel faster than the solvent front
The solvent would rise past the spot without touching it
The paper would absorb solvent unevenly on each side
Otherwise the ink dissolves into the solvent instead of travelling up the paper
questions.explanation: If the spot is submerged it simply washes into the solvent and no separation occurs.

questions.stem: Which mixture could NOT be separated by filtration?
questions.explanation: Dissolved substances pass through the filter. All the others are suspended solids.

questions.stem: How would you tell a pure substance from a mixture using melting point?
options: A pure substance melts sharply at one temperature; a mixture melts over a range
A mixture melts sharply and a pure substance does not
Both melt at exactly the same temperature
questions.explanation: A sharp, fixed melting point is strong evidence of purity — the standard laboratory test.

questions.stem: Why does adding more solute eventually stop dissolving?
options: The solution becomes saturated at that temperature
The solvent turns into a solid
questions.explanation: A saturated solution holds as much solute as it can at that temperature. Heating usually allows more.

questions.stem: Which separation technique relies on a difference in density?
options: Using a separating funnel for oil and water
questions.explanation: Immiscible liquids form layers by density, and the lower one is tapped off first.

questions.stem: Why does sea water boil at slightly above 100 °C?
options: Sea water is a pure substance
Dissolved salt raises the boiling point of the solution
questions.explanation: Dissolved solute raises boiling point and lowers freezing point — the same principle behind salting roads in winter.

questions.stem: A distillation collects a liquid at a steady 78 °C, then the temperature rises. What does this indicate?
options: One component has finished distilling and another is beginning
questions.explanation: A steady plateau marks one component distilling over. The rise signals a change to the next.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best show that a colourless liquid is pure water rather than a solution?
options: It freezes somewhere close to 0 °C and stays completely clear while cooling
It dissolves salt and sugar readily, which pure water does faster than tap water
It boils sharply at exactly 100 °C at standard pressure and leaves no residue on evaporation
It has no measurable taste or odour when compared against a sample of tap water
questions.explanation: Appearance proves nothing — dissolved salt is invisible. A sharp boiling point and no residue are the real tests.

questions.stem: Why is fractional distillation needed for liquids with similar boiling points?
options: Similar boiling points cannot be separated at all
Repeated evaporation and condensation up a column gives a much better separation
Simple distillation cannot heat liquids enough
questions.explanation: The fractionating column effectively repeats the distillation many times, which is what separates close-boiling components like crude oil fractions.

questions.stem: A mixture separates into layers on standing. What can you conclude about its components?
options: They do not mix and have different densities
questions.explanation: Layering is a sign of immiscible substances of different densities — a heterogeneous mixture, not a solution.

questions.stem: Why can compounds not be separated by physical means but mixtures can?
options: A compound's components are chemically bonded; a mixture's are not
questions.explanation: Breaking chemical bonds requires a chemical reaction. Physical methods only exploit differences in physical properties.

questions.stem: Chromatography of a green ink gives blue and yellow spots. What does this show?
options: The green ink is a mixture of at least two coloured substances
The ink was contaminated by the paper
Green is not a real colour
The solvent changed the ink chemically
questions.explanation: Separation into distinct spots demonstrates the original was a mixture. Chromatography separates, it does not react.

questions.stem: What is a suspension?
options: A solution where the solid has dissolved
A mixture where solid particles are spread through a liquid but settle over time
questions.explanation: Muddy water is a suspension: the particles stay visible and eventually settle. A solution never settles.

questions.stem: What is an insoluble substance?
options: One that does not dissolve in a given solvent
questions.explanation: Sand is insoluble in water, so it can be filtered out.

questions.stem: What is the solvent in most everyday solutions?
questions.explanation: Water dissolves so many substances that it is often called the universal solvent.
questions.teaching:
A solution has two parts, and the words for them are decided by which is doing the dissolving.

Whatever gets dissolved is the solute; whatever it dissolves into is the solvent. The solvent is normally the component present in the greater amount, and it keeps its state — dissolve a solid into a liquid and you still have a liquid. One substance dissolves such an extraordinary range of things that it is called the universal solvent, and it is why biology happens in it, why rivers carry minerals, and why most everyday solutions are the kind they are.

questions.stem: What is a saturated solution?
options: One holding as much dissolved solute as it can at that temperature
One with no solute in it
questions.explanation: Adding more solute to a saturated solution simply leaves it undissolved.

questions.stem: What is evaporation used for in separating mixtures?
options: Removing a liquid to leave a dissolved solid behind
questions.explanation: The liquid leaves as vapour and the dissolved solid stays.

questions.stem: Which piece of equipment is used to separate two immiscible liquids?
questions.explanation: The layers are tapped off separately, lower layer first.

questions.stem: What does 'immiscible' mean?
options: Two liquids that do not mix and form separate layers
A solid that will not dissolve
A gas that cannot be compressed
questions.explanation: Oil and water are immiscible. Liquids that do mix are miscible.

questions.stem: What is distillate?
options: The liquid collected after being evaporated and condensed
questions.explanation: In distillation the distillate is the purified product.

questions.stem: Which mixture is a solution?
questions.explanation: Only the sugar dissolves to give a uniform mixture.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a filter paper's small pores?
options: To let liquid and dissolved particles through while trapping larger solids
questions.explanation: Separation is by particle size, which is why dissolved substances pass straight through.

questions.stem: Why does a solution look uniform even under a microscope?
options: The particles settle out of sight
The dissolved particles are individual and far too small to see
questions.explanation: Dissolving separates the solute into individual particles, unlike a suspension where clumps remain.

questions.stem: Why is chromatography paper marked with a pencil line rather than pen?
options: Pencil graphite does not dissolve and travel with the solvent
questions.explanation: Ink would separate along with the samples and ruin the result.

questions.stem: Which property is exploited when separating a mixture by distillation?
questions.explanation: The component with the lower boiling point vaporises first.

questions.stem: Why does crystallisation give purer crystals when the solvent evaporates slowly?
options: Slow growth allows a more regular structure that excludes impurities
Slow evaporation lowers the solution's temperature
questions.explanation: Rapid crystallisation traps impurities in the growing crystal.

questions.stem: A mixture of alcohol and water is distilled. Which is collected first and why?
options: Water, because it is more common
Alcohol, because it has the lower boiling point
questions.explanation: The lower-boiling component vaporises first, so it is collected first.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to know whether a mixture is homogeneous before choosing a separation method?
options: Uniform mixtures need methods that work on dissolved substances, not filtration
All mixtures separate the same way
questions.explanation: Filtration and decanting work on heterogeneous mixtures; solutions require distillation, evaporation or chromatography.

questions.stem: Which everyday process is essentially filtration?
questions.explanation: A colander traps solids too large to pass through, letting liquid drain.

questions.stem: Why is 'pure' used differently in science and in advertising?
options: Science means a single substance; advertising often means natural or unadulterated
Science has no definition of pure
questions.explanation: 'Pure orange juice' is chemically a complex mixture, which is a useful example of technical versus everyday vocabulary.

questions.stem: Two students separate the same mixture and get different masses of recovered salt. What is the most likely cause?
options: Mass is not conserved in separations
Some product was lost during transfer or some water remained
The salt changed into another substance
questions.explanation: Practical losses are the usual explanation. Mass is conserved, but not all of it is recovered.

questions.stem: Why does adding salt to icy roads work?
options: Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point of water, so ice melts at lower temperatures
questions.explanation: Depression of freezing point is a property of solutions, and it is the same principle that raises boiling point.

questions.stem: A chromatogram shows one spot for a substance claimed to be a mixture. What can you conclude?
options: Under these conditions no separation occurred, so it may be pure or the method may be unsuitable
questions.explanation: A single spot is consistent with purity, but a poorly chosen solvent can also fail to separate components — a good example of a method's limits.

questions.stem: Why is fractional distillation used for crude oil rather than simple distillation?
options: Crude oil boils at a single fixed temperature
Simple distillation cannot reach high enough temperatures
Crude oil is a pure substance
Crude oil contains many components with overlapping boiling ranges
questions.explanation: The fractionating column separates a continuum of hydrocarbons into useful fractions.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support the claim that dissolving is a physical change?
options: The dissolved substance can be recovered unchanged by evaporating the solvent
questions.explanation: Recovering the original substance unchanged is the test. Disappearing from view and temperature changes happen in chemical changes too.

questions.stem: What is a colloid?
options: A solution in which the solvent is a gas rather than a liquid at room temperature
A mixture with particles too small to settle but larger than in a solution
A mixture whose particles settle out slowly if it is left standing undisturbed
A substance made of two elements chemically bonded in a fixed whole-number ratio
questions.explanation: Milk and fog are colloids: they look uniform but scatter light.

questions.stem: Which method separates a magnetic solid from a non-magnetic one?
questions.explanation: The property exploited is magnetism, not particle size.

questions.stem: What is a solute in a cup of tea with sugar?
questions.explanation: The sugar dissolves, so it is the solute.
questions.teaching:
The two components of a solution are named by their roles rather than by what they are.

Whatever dissolves is the solute; whatever it dissolves into is the solvent. In a cup of tea there are several dissolved substances at once — the compounds extracted from the leaves, plus anything stirred in afterwards — and all of them are solutes, with the water acting as the solvent for all of them. A useful check: heat the mixture until the liquid has gone, and whatever remains behind was the dissolved component.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'miscible'?
options: Two liquids that mix completely in any proportion
questions.explanation: Alcohol and water are miscible; oil and water are not.

questions.stem: What does a filter funnel hold?
options: Filter paper, through which the mixture is poured
questions.explanation: The funnel supports the paper and directs the filtrate.

questions.stem: What is a solvent front in chromatography?
options: The furthest point the solvent has travelled up the paper
questions.explanation: Distances are measured relative to the solvent front.

questions.stem: Which is a pure substance: gold or brass?
questions.explanation: Gold is an element; brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, so a mixture.
questions.teaching:
Purity in chemistry means something stricter than in everyday speech: a pure substance contains only one kind of particle throughout.

Elements qualify, and so do compounds, because a compound has one fixed composition all the way through. A mixture does not, however evenly it is blended — an alloy is metals melted together in proportions that can be varied, so it is a mixture even though it looks completely uniform. That is the test to apply here: is this made of one substance, or several combined without bonding into a new one?

questions.stem: What happens to a solution's concentration as more solvent is added?
questions.explanation: Diluting spreads the same solute through more solvent.

questions.stem: What is a residue left after filtering muddy water?
options: The mud trapped in the paper
questions.explanation: Residue stays behind; filtrate passes through.

questions.stem: Why is sand described as insoluble in water?
options: It does not dissolve, and settles or can be filtered out
questions.explanation: Insoluble substances remain as separate particles.

questions.stem: How could you separate iron filings, sand and salt from each other?
options: Magnet for iron, then dissolve the salt and filter off the sand, then evaporate
Filter, then distil, then use a magnet
questions.explanation: Each step exploits a different property in a sensible order.

questions.stem: Why does a solution not separate on standing while a suspension does?
options: Solutions are transparent and suspensions are opaque, and it is that difference which keeps them apart
Solute particles are individual and stay dispersed; suspension particles are large enough to settle
A solution is chemically bonded throughout, while a suspension is only a physical mixture of two parts
Solute particles are lighter than the liquid, while suspended particles are always denser than it
questions.explanation: Particle size is the key difference.

questions.stem: Why is the boiling point of a mixture usually a range rather than a single value?
options: Different components boil at different temperatures
questions.explanation: This is why a sharp boiling point indicates purity.

questions.stem: Why must a distillation flask not be filled too full?
options: Boiling liquid could splash into the condenser and contaminate the distillate
The vapour would condense before reaching the condenser
The thermometer would sit below the liquid surface
questions.explanation: Bumping carries impurities over, defeating the purpose of the separation.

questions.stem: A solution is cooled and crystals form. What does this show?
options: Solubility usually decreases as temperature falls
questions.explanation: Less solute can stay dissolved at lower temperature, so the excess crystallises out.

questions.stem: Which observation shows that a liquid is a mixture rather than a pure substance?
options: It boils over a range of temperatures
questions.explanation: Boiling behaviour is a physical test that appearance cannot substitute for.

questions.stem: Why does adding a solute change both the boiling and freezing points of a solvent?
options: Solutes are chemically bonded to the solvent
Solute particles interfere with the solvent particles changing state
questions.explanation: Boiling point rises and freezing point falls — collectively called colligative properties.

questions.stem: Two chromatograms use different solvents and give different spot patterns. What does this show?
options: Separation depends on the solvent as well as the substances
questions.explanation: Choosing an appropriate solvent is part of designing the method.

questions.stem: Why can distillation purify water contaminated with bacteria as well as salt?
options: Only the water vapourises; the bacteria and salt remain behind
questions.explanation: Anything non-volatile stays in the flask, which is why distilled water is both salt-free and sterile.

questions.stem: Why is it inaccurate to say filtration 'purifies' water?
options: It removes suspended solids but leaves dissolved substances and many microbes
questions.explanation: A clear filtrate can still contain dissolved salts and pathogens.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best distinguish a colloid from a true solution?
options: A beam of light is visible passing through the colloid but not the solution
questions.explanation: Larger colloid particles scatter light — the Tyndall effect — while dissolved particles do not.
